## Answer: 355

This rests on S(n) = n²/4 for even n and S(n) = 0 for odd n. I derived the construction and the parity facts, but I did not fully prove the upper bound. The key step I could not verify is that a black-start family and a white-start family cannot both be Hamiltonian in one configuration.

**Odd n.** A good cell needs a closed walk of n² unit moves on the grid, which is bipartite, so n² must be even. Hence S(n) = 0 for odd n.

**Even n: lower bound.** Let c = v₀ be good, with Hamiltonian cycle v₀, …, v_{N−1} (N = n²) and direction dⱼ from vⱼ to vⱼ₊₁. Since the arrow at vⱼ at time t is Rᵗ(a(vⱼ)), where R is the 90° counterclockwise rotation, the configuration must have a(vⱼ) = R^{−j}(dⱼ). Because N ≡ 0 (mod 4), indices are consistent mod 4.

Take any m. At time s, Turbo sits at v_{4m+s} and the arrow there is R^{s−(4m+s)}(d_{4m+s}) = d_{4m+s}. So Turbo follows the same cycle, and every vⱼ with j ≡ 0 (mod 4) is good. That gives N/4 = n²/4 good cells.

**Even n: upper bound (partial).** Any good cell lies on a state-cycle of length N in the space of (cell, time mod 4). Each such cycle contributes exactly N/4 good cells, and the cycles are checkerboard-typed. Two cycles of the same type are impossible: at every cell their outgoing directions would be opposite, which fails at a corner. So a configuration has at most one black-type and one white-type family. I did not rule out the mixed case, which would give n²/2. A search over ρ-symmetric configurations for n = 4 found no Hamiltonian trajectory, and a direct check for n = 2 gives S(2) = 1 = n²/4, consistent with the bound n²/4.

**Sum.** For even n from 10 to 20, n²/4 = 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, which sums to 355.

ANSWER: 355
